title: Keep Pēpi (Baby) Healthy
description: Learn about the various methods healthcare providers use to monitor your pēpi's health and development throughout pregnancy.

contentSections.title: Smoking/nutrition in pregnancy
contentSections.content:
Key risks of smoking in pregnancy:
  • Increased risk of miscarriage and stillbirth.
  • Higher likelihood of preterm birth and low birth weight.
  • Increased chance of newborn respiratory problems, ear infections, and longer-term health issues (e.g. asthma).
  • Higher risk of Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy (SUDI) / Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) when carers smoke during pregnancy or around the pēpi.
Guidance & practical points:
  • Quitting smoking at any stage of pregnancy provides benefit; earlier is better, but stopping even later helps the pēpi.
  • Electronic cigarettes (vaping) are not guaranteed to be safe during pregnancy — discuss with a health professional. Nicotine itself affects fetal oxygen supply.
  • Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) may be considered under clinical advice; discuss risks/benefits with your lead maternity carer (LMC) or doctor. Clinical support is available to help with a safe quit plan.
  • Whānau / partner smoking also matters — reduce household smoke exposure and create a smoke-free home/car for pēpi’s health.
Support & services:
  • Quitline and local stop-smoking services provide free or low-cost counselling and support tailored for pregnant people.
  • Ask your LMC, midwife, GP or local public-health service for referrals and guidance.

contentSections.title: Healthy eating when pregnant
contentSections.content:
Overall healthy eating principles:
  • Choose a variety of foods from the four main food groups each day:
    • Vegetables and fruit
    • Breads, cereals and other starchy foods (prefer wholegrain where possible)
    • Milk, yoghurt and hard cheese (or any cheese made from pasteurised milk)
    • Lean meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, legumes, nuts and seeds (or plant-based protein alternatives)
  • “Eating for two” is a myth — energy needs increase modestly during pregnancy. Aim for a balanced, nutrient-dense diet rather than large extra quantities of low-nutrient foods.
  • Stay well hydrated — typical advice is around 8–9 cups of fluids per day (adjust for activity, climate, vomiting, etc.).
Food safety — important during pregnancy:
  • Avoid high-risk foods such as raw or undercooked meats, raw fish/sushi (unless heat-treated), raw eggs, some soft cheeses or unpasteurised dairy, and deli meats unless heated thoroughly.
  • Follow safe food handling/storage to reduce foodborne illness risk.
Key nutrients to watch (and common sources):
  • Folate / Folic acid — critical early in pregnancy to reduce neural tube defects. Found in fortified breads/cereals, legumes, green leafy vegetables; supplements commonly recommended before conception and in early pregnancy.
  • Iodine — important for pēpi’s brain development. Sources: fortified bread (in NZ), dairy, seafood; supplementation is often recommended where intake may be low.
  • Iron — supports maternal blood volume and pēpi’s iron stores. Sources: red meat, poultry, fish, legumes, fortified cereals; vitamin C helps iron absorption. Vegetarians may need to pay special attention to iron and may require supplements after testing/advice.
  • Vitamin B12 — essential, especially for vegetarian/vegan pregnant people; found in animal products and fortified foods — vegans usually require B12 supplementation.
  • Calcium — for maternal bone health and fetal skeletal development. Sources: milk, yoghurt, cheese or fortified plant milks and alternatives.
  • Vitamin D — recommended in some cases; discuss testing/supplementation with your health provider.
  • Omega-3 (DHA/EPA) — supports brain development. Sources: oily fish (but observe fish safety limits), and algal DHA supplements for vegans/vegetarians.
Vegetarian / vegan / alternative diets:
  • Well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets can be compatible with a healthy pregnancy but require attention to certain nutrients (B12, iron, iodine, DHA, protein, calcium, vitamin D).
  • Consider discussing with your LMC or a registered dietitian/nutritionist to review your diet, obtain relevant blood tests (iron, B12, vitamin D as needed), and to consider appropriate supplementation.
  • Fortified foods (e.g., fortified plant milks, breads, cereals) and appropriate supplements (especially B12 and possibly iodine/DHA) are commonly advised for strict plant-based diets.

If you have special conditions (e.g., gestational diabetes, food allergies, very low BMI or rapid weight gain), you should ask your LMC or a dietitian for an individualised plan.
